normalized_proposition: CBAM complements the EU ETS and replaces specified free-allocation mechanisms to address carbon leakage; this is a formal inter-scheme connection.
Goods are imported only by an authorised CBAM declarant; applicants apply before importing; status is granted by the competent authority on listed criteria.
Each authorised declarant submits an annual CBAM declaration (by 31 May) and surrenders certificates corresponding to verified declared emissions.
Operators of third-country installations may be registered in the registry on request, determine embedded emissions and ensure verification; their duties are distinct from the declarant's.
Embedded emissions must be verified by an accredited verifier under the Annex VI principles; accreditation follows Reg. 2018/2067 or accreditation by a national accreditation body.
The Commission establishes the CBAM registry, which carries declarant and certificate information and is available to customs and competent authorities.
Customs authorities do not allow importation by non-authorised declarants and periodically transmit specified import data to the Commission.
The Commission has the oversight role in review of declarations; competent authorities may also review; risk-based review strategy and information exchange.
Delegated acts are conferred on the Commission subject to revocation and objection by Parliament and Council; implementing acts follow the examination procedure referred to in Art. 29(2).
Authorisation, review and penalty decisions are bound by enumerated criteria, risk-based triggers, ranges and factors.
Circumvention may be notified to the Commission by Member States and affected or interested parties; the Commission may investigate on notification or on its own determination.
Declarants must keep records sufficiently detailed to enable verification and review.
Penalty decisions are notified with the conclusion of non-compliance, reasons and amount.
The Commission reports to the European Parliament and the Council on application and review.

Additional statement-level evidence propositions in provisions not individually anchored in V8's claims (e.g. Art. 2(6)–(12) and Annex III; Art. 17(4)–(9) guarantee and registration; Art. 20–24 sale/price/repurchase/cancellation; Art. 31 free-allocation adjustment; Art. 32–36).

An importer or indirect customs representative applies to the competent authority of the Member State of establishment; the authority consults other competent authorities and the Commission and grants or refuses status on the Art. 17(2) criteria.

Guarantee and revocation: the competent authority requires a guarantee where the applicant was not established for two financial years, may require an additional or replacement guarantee, releases it, and revokes the status on request, when criteria cease to be met, or after serious or repeated infringement of surrender/quarterly-sufficiency obligations, after hearing the declarant and a consultation procedure.
The Commission sets up the declarant's registry account once authorisation is granted, grants access to it, and closes it on cessation or revocation.
Operators are registered in the registry on request, notified, must report changes, may be deregistered, and may disclose verified data to declarants.

Declarants and operators must ensure verification of declared or determined emissions by an accredited verifier, who prepares a verification report applying the Annex VI principles; declarants may use verified operator information.
A national accreditation body accredits a person as verifier on request; persons accredited under Reg. 2018/2067 are accredited verifiers.

Declaration and surrender: whether the duty to submit the declaration and to surrender certificates is a relation toward an identified counterparty (and which), or a duty with the registry as channel and no counterparty named (the Commission being named only as remover of surrendered certificates).
Customs authorities bar importation by non-authorised persons and transmit specified import data to the Commission, which forwards it to the competent authority.
The Commission maintains the registry and makes information available automatically and in real time to customs and competent authorities; public information; confidentiality with sharing derogation.

Commission review of CBAM declarations: whether the Commission's review relation is directed at the declarant (reviewed party) with results communicated to the competent authority, or is a relation toward the competent authority.
The competent authority imposes the penalty after determining non-compliance, notifies conclusion, reasons and amount, secures payment, and communicates penalty decisions to the Commission.

Determination and sufficiency: on the Commission's preliminary calculation the competent authority determines the number of certificates that should have been surrendered and requests surrender; the Commission informs the competent authority of insufficient quarterly certificate balances (80% rule) and the authority notifies the declarant.

Certificate lifecycle: a Member State sells certificates on the common central platform to authorised declarants established there; the Commission runs the platform, records each sale in the declarant's account, repurchases on behalf of the Member State, and cancels remaining certificates annually (with suspension while a surrender number is disputed).

Circumvention: Member States and affected or interested parties may notify the Commission; the Commission initiates an investigation on a compliant notification or on its own determination, may be assisted by competent and customs authorities, and notifies competent authorities.
Delegation control: Parliament and Council confer, may revoke and may object to delegated acts; the Commission consults Member State experts and notifies adoption.
The Commission is assisted by the CBAM Committee in adopting implementing acts under the examination procedure.
The Commission presents reports and, where appropriate, legislative proposals to Parliament and Council before the end of the transitional period and periodically thereafter.
The Commission assesses, in its biennial report, the implementation and administration of authorisation by Member States and the functioning of the CBAM.

Third-country conditional exemption: a third country submits reports; the Commission assesses and may remove it; the Commission adopts delegated acts on the Annex III list and requirements; the Union may conclude carbon-pricing agreements.
Member States designate competent authorities and inform the Commission; the Commission publishes the list and assists and coordinates; competent authorities exchange information.

Transitional reporting: customs authorities inform importers of the reporting duty; importers (or indirect customs representatives) submit quarterly CBAM reports to the Commission; the Commission transmits lists/indicative information to competent authorities, which run the correction procedure and impose penalties.

Qualification of reasoned decisions that carry information about appeal (refusal, revocation, determination, penalty): formal answerability/procedural safeguard, or information with sufficiency indeterminate because no forum, assessment capacity or consequence is stated.

Authorisation and import access: application, Commission/authority consultation, status decision, registry entry and account, customs barrier, and (where included) guarantee and revocation form one arrangement.

Partition of emissions-assurance relations: operator registration and disclosure, accreditation and verification, and the declarant's declaration form either one arrangement of calculation, assurance and reporting, or distinct arrangements (registration/disclosure; accreditation–verification; declaration and surrender).

Registry-mediated administrative oversight: customs data, registry availability, Commission review and communication to competent authorities form one arrangement, versus an information-transmission arrangement (customs → Commission → competent authority, with secrecy) distinct from review/determination/sanction relations.

Certificates and obligations: certificate pricing, sale, holding, surrender and consequences form one arrangement, versus a certificate life-cycle arrangement (price, sale, repurchase, cancellation) distinct from the obligation–review–determination–sanction arrangement, with overlap.

Rule-making, review, circumvention and reporting: delegated/implementing-act control, circumvention, third-country scope management and Commission reporting form one arrangement of rule-making, coordination and periodic evaluation, versus four distinct arrangements (delegation control; circumvention; third-country listing; reports), with overlaps.
Third-country listing and conditional electricity exemption form an arrangement (conditions, third-country reports, Commission assessment, removal, delegated acts).
Transitional reporting (Arts. 32–35: information, quarterly reports, indicative input, correction, penalty) forms a bounded arrangement.

Overlap among arrangements: V8's arrangements share component relations (R03 in CFG2/CFG4; R07 in CFG3/CFG4; R08 in CFG3/CFG5) without classification; RGAM records overlap between SC-01/05/06, SC-02/03, SC-04/05 and SC-08 with SC-07/09/10.

The Regulation constitutes a formal governance architecture linking authorisation, declaration/surrender and the certificate lifecycle with review, determination and sanction (bounded to the Regulation; formal design only).

Whether the verification and accreditation relations (Arts. 8, 10(5), 18, Annex VI) are inside the same architecture as authorisation, declaration/surrender, certificates and enforcement, given that the status of the accredited verifier and accreditation body depends on instruments outside the Regulation.

Whether the Commission's rule-making relations (delegation control and committee-assisted implementing acts) are part of the architecture as a control structure; and whether the committee's involvement under the examination procedure (Reg. 182/2011) constitutes an additional check.

Whether the transitional reporting regime (Arts. 32–35) belongs in the same architecture as the definitive-period regime, given that the text couples them only by temporal succession and the transitional period ended on 31 December 2025.

Whether the circumvention (Art. 27) and third-country listing/exemption (Art. 2(6)–(12)) arrangements are part of the same architecture, are separate arrangements with no stated consequence/coupling, or (for the exemption) a norm-only integrated arrangement.

Number and boundary of architectures: one formal architecture covering Arts. 4–30 and 32–35, versus an integrated core (authorisation, certificates, obligations/enforcement) with overlapping verification and delegation arrangements and unintegrated transitional, circumvention and reporting arrangements, with a single whole-instrument architecture not warranted.

Centralisation/vertical distribution: information infrastructure, accounts, price, platform and review input rest with the Commission; binding status, determination, penalty and sale decisions rest with Member State authorities; neither a 'centralised' nor a 'hybrid' label for the whole.
Discretion distribution: bounded discretion in authorisation (criteria), review (risk strategy), penalty (range and factors); indicative Commission output versus binding competent-authority decision.

Accountability as an architectural property: the Commission and authorities distribute 'answerability' across positions (V8), versus no actor–forum accountability relation coded in the Regulation, with the architecture-level claim undetermined because appeals and judicial control are governed outside it (RGAM).

Public/private character of verifiers: the architecture spans 'accredited private verifiers', versus the allocation of verification along the public–private axis being undeterminable within the Regulation.

Whether the status of authorised CBAM declarant is a necessary stage for all importation within scope, given scope derogations (Art. 2(3)–(4), Art. 5(4)) resting on thresholds defined outside the Regulation.
Intermediation: importers not established in a Member State apply and report only through an indirect customs representative; verification is intermediated by accredited verifiers.

Plurality of decision centres: each Member State designates its own competent authority and the competent authority of the Member State of establishment decides; delegated-act control is held independently by Parliament and Council.

Absence-dependent statements recorded only by RGAM: the indirect customs representative's substitutability is undetermined (PROP-018); no rule-making power is conferred on private actors (PROP-010); no qualified relation couples the transitional and definitive regimes beyond temporal succession (CL-07); no consequence of an investigation is stated (ARCH-06).
Relational depth of the enforcement sequence: Commission review and assessment → preliminary calculation → determination and surrender request → penalty → recovery.
The claims concern formal legal design; implementation, practice, effectiveness and the relative practical centrality of actors are not asserted.

Penalty amounts, the certificate price base, free-allocation adjustment and means of recovery rest partly on instruments outside the Regulation (Directive 2003/87/EC, Reg. 1031/2010, national law); claims about them should or should not be limited to what the Regulation states.

Rival groupings and boundary sensitivities for the architecture: status conferral as a separate architecture; obligations split from enforcement; certificate market as a separate architecture; delegated and implementing acts as two architectures; transitional regime as an earlier phase; one architecture versus distinguishable architectures.

Temporal reference and validity: RGAM states legal status at the reference date 2026-01-01 (transitional norms bounded, last quarterly report only); V8 states no reference date and treats the whole instrument as one formal design.

Stopping level: both arms stop at the architectural level (no regime claim); RGAM stops below the architectural level (INDETERMINATE) for verification, transitional, delegation and circumvention arrangements where V8 includes them.

Confidence in the architecture claim is qualified: medium-high for existence and broad organisation, lower for centrality (V8); outcomes provisional and corpus-scoped with unvalidated I2/I3 thresholds (RGAM).
Higher-order constructs: governance logic, strategy, regime or architecture-among-regimes beyond the architecture.
The full accountability chain and available remedies are not resolved by the Regulation alone.
Use and reliability of default versus actual emissions values cannot be evaluated from the legal text.
Direction/counterparty uncertainty where the text states no recipient or obligor (e.g. certified person in Art. 9(2)/Annex IV 5(e), recipient information in Art. 25(5)).
